Art
Cars

A horizontal timeline
of 65 works, 1925–2025

Ever since its invention, the automobile has had an irresistible pull on the human imagination—and that’s especially true when artists do the imagining. In their visionary hands, motorized vehicles of all kinds become more than simple transportation, luxurious status symbols, or engineering marvels. They become canvases for art and vivid reflections of their cultural moments.

The wall runs left to right in chronological order, from Sonia Delaunay’s painted Citroën B12 to Nina Chanel Abney’s Chevrolet C10—a century of artists treating the car as a surface, a sculpture, a proposition.

Drawn from the Art Cars Handbook
Edited by Larry Warsh · No More Rulers, 2026
Scroll
1920s
1925

Sonia Delaunay

Untitled, 1925
1925 Citroën B12

As a key figure in the early 20th-century Parisian avant-garde, SONIA DELAUNAY (b. 1885, Gradizhsk, Ukraine–d. 1979, Paris) was known for her bold use of color and geometric forms, working in disciplines ranging from painting and textile design to fashion. A pioneer of automotive art, she brought her vibrant abstract vision to the automobile decades before the term “art car” entered popular usage. In 1925, she covered a Citroën B12 in vivid painted rectangles that would have become blurs of color as the car gained speed. An iconic photograph captures Delaunay standing next to the Citroën. Her chic ensemble is made in a fabric of her own design that matches the car.

01
1960s
1963 / 2014

Christo & Jeanne-Claude

Wrapped 1961 Volkswagen Beetle Saloon, 1963/2014
1961 Volkswagen, tarpaulin with grommets, ropes

Internationally renowned for wrapping buildings and landscapes, CHRISTO (b. Christo Vladimirov Javacheff, 1935, Gabrovo, Bulgaria–d. 2020, New York City) was a young artist experimenting with this technique in the early 1960s, along with his partner, JEANNE-CLAUDE (b. Jeanne-Claude Denat de Buillebon, 1935, d. 2009, New York City). Having fled Communist Bulgaria in 1957, Christo was fascinated by Western consumer objects and sought to transform them through concealment. Still recognizable beneath layers of fabric, the duo’s Wrapped 1961 Volkswagen Beetle Saloon (1963/2014) has been stripped of its utility as a vehicle and converted into pure form. That tension between revealing and concealing, between the everyday and the monumental, would define Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s art practice in the decades to come.

02
1967

Sonia Delaunay

Untitled, 1967
1967 Matra M530

In 1967, SONIA DELAUNAY made a late-career return to automotive art with a commission from Jean-Luc Lagardère, CEO of the French sportscar manufacturer Matra. In designing the work, Delaunay approached the mid-engined Matra 530 as a kinetic canvas. She again devised a pattern of brightly colored shapes, which would resolve into a light blue tone when the vehicle was in motion. As a thoughtful consideration of safety—creating a pattern that would not distract other drivers—Delaunay’s late-life art car reflects her sophisticated understanding of art and its relationship to function.

03
1967

Arman

Untitled (Renault), 1967
1967 Renault 4

ARMAN (b. 1928, Nice, France–d. 2005, New York City) was a French-American artist known for bold explorations of accumulation, destruction, and consumer culture. His kaleidoscopic Untitled (Renault) (1967) covers the exterior of a humble Renault 4 with 819 carefully placed drawings of the car itself, turning it into a mesmerizing exploration of repetition and accumulation. Commissioned as a fundraiser by a French magazine to benefit medical research, Arman’s work was an early entry in the Art Car movement, created years before BMW began its celebrated Art Car series.

04
1969

Pippa Garner

Kar-Mann (Half Human Half Car), 1969
Mixed media, two versions (1969; 1969/2024)

PIPPA GARNER (b. 1942, Evanston, Illinois–d. 2024, Los Angeles) was a conceptual artist whose reimagined consumer products are witty critiques of American car culture, gender, and the plasticity of the human body. Created as an art-school final project, the small sculpture Kar-Mann (Half Human Half Car) (1969) features a features a human lower half fused with the front of a miniature Volkswagen Karmann Ghia. With one leg lifted suggestively over a map of Detroit—heart of the automotive industry—it was enough to get Garner expelled from the ArtCenter College of Design’s transportation design program, and to launch a career exploring gender fluidity and consumer culture.

05
1970s
1975

Alexander Calder

BMW Art Car 1, 1975
1975 BMW 3.0 CSL

When French racing driver and auctioneer Hervé Poulain envisioned a melding of art and motorsport, he turned to internationally renowned artist ALEXANDER CALDER (b. 1898, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania–d. 1976, New York City). Poulain’s invitation for Calder to paint a BMW racing car led to the creation of the first BMW Art Car in 1975. Calder transformed the BMW 3.0 CSL into a dynamic canvas, using broad swaths of color to create the illusion of movement. As one of his final works, Calder’s BMW Art Car is a culmination of his lifelong exploration of motion, engineering, and creative expression.

06
1976

Frank Stella

BMW Art Car 2, 1976
1976 BMW 3.0 CS

In 1976, artist FRANK STELLA (b. 1936, Malden, Massachusetts–d. 2024, New York City) was commissioned to create the second BMW Art Car. Like the first BMW Art Car done by Alexander Calder, Stella’s was a BMW 3.0 racing car, and like Calder’s the year before, Stella’s car competed in the 24-hour race in Le Mans, France. Explaining his idea for the car, Stella noted that the overall design is “from a drawing on graph paper,” adding that “when it’s morphed over the car’s forms it becomes interesting.” On the background grid, Stella superimposed bold black lines tracing various shapes, including angled forms and spirals. The effect, he said, “is like a blueprint transferred onto the bodywork.”

07
1977

Roy Lichtenstein

BMW Art Car 3, 1977
1977 BMW 320i Group 5 Race Version

ROY LICHTENSTEIN (b. 1923, New York City–d. 1997, New York City) was a leading figure in American Pop Art, known for exploring the convergence of fine art, advertising, and consumerism. In 1977, his brought his signature comic-book-inspired style to the third work in the celebrated BMW Art Car series. Using vibrant colors, Ben-Day dots, and graphic “speedlines,” Lichtenstein transformed the vehicle into a dynamic canvas suggesting movement even while stationary. Abstract representations of landscape, sun, sky, and road evoke the environment through which the car was driven.

08
1978

Ettore Sottsass

Alfa Romeo Giulietta Punk, 1978
Alfa Romeo Giulietta

ETTORE SOTTSASS (b. 1917, Innsbruck, Austria–d. 2007, Milan, Italy) was an Italian architect and designer whose bold, unconventional work helped define postmodern design. Best known as the founder of the Memphis Group in 1981, Sottsass rejected modernist minimalism in favor of vibrant color, playful geometry, and emotional expression. Those qualities are apparent in his Alfa Romeo Giulietta Punk car, created in collaboration with Alfa Romeo and the Italian fashion company Fiorucci. Hand-painted and adorned with upholstered blue bumpers, the car features a custom interior, including carved wood elements and gauges with measurements in colors rather than numbers.

09
1979

Andy Warhol

BMW Art Car 4, 1979
1979 BMW M1 Group 4 Race Version

The M1 by ANDY WARHOL (b. 1928, Pittsburgh–d. 1987, New York City) is an iconic work in the BMW Art Car series. A pioneering figure of the Pop Art movement, Warhol often explored themes of mass production, celebrity, and modern culture, blurring the line between commercial imagery and fine art. Unlike previous BMW Art Car artists, whose designs were transposed onto the vehicles by technicians and assistants, Warhol insisted on painting the car himself. Applying broad, expressive brushstrokes, he reportedly completed the design in less than half an hour, capturing the blur of movement and speed of a racing car in action.

10
1980s
1981

Jean-Michel Basquiat

Untitled, 1981
1980 Cadillac “Bustle Back” Sedan de Ville

In the winter of 1980-81, shooting began in Lower Manhattan on a film about the downtown art scene. The star was a young, not-yet-famous artist: JEAN-MICHEL BASQUIAT. Twenty years later the movie was released as Downtown 81 (2000). Late in the film, Jean finds a suitcase full of money and uses it to buy a Cadillac from a stranger on the street. “Jean pulls out a gold magic marker and starts to write ‘Gold Wood’” on the car, recalls the artist Maripol, who produced the film. “Basquiat’s poetry, his writing, is not easy to translate,” she says. “In ‘Gold Wood’ one can ask, What is paper made of? Wood. It is so much simpler for his genius mind to write ‘Gold Wood’ than ‘Money.’”

11
1983

Keith Haring

Untitled (Land Rover Defender), 1983
1971 Series III Land Rover Defender

KEITH HARING (b. 1958, Reading, Pennsylvania–d. 1990, New York City) was an artist, activist, and cultural figure known for his boldly graphic, figurative iconography. Rooted in the street culture and activism of 1980s New York, his work fused art, music, and social justice into a universally accessible visual vocabulary. In Untitled (Land Rover Defender), Haring covered a 1971 Land Rover with his signature imagery, including elements from his 1983 poster design for the Montreux Jazz Festival. The car remained in Haring’s personal collection and was not publicly exhibited until after his death in 1990.

12
1984

Kenny Scharf

Suprema Ultima Deluxa Van Chrome Cadillac, 1984
1961 Cadillac Sedan de Ville, mixed media

A vibrant, cartoon-inspired aesthetic animates the art of KENNY SCHARF (b. 1958, Los Angeles), who emerged as a key figure in New York’s East Village art scene of the 1980s. Working under the alias Van Chrome, Scharf transformed a 1961 Cadillac Sedan de Ville into Suprema Ultima Deluxa Van Chrome Cadillac (1984). In eye-popping color, he covered the car inside and out with cosmic imagery, cartoons, plastic dinosaurs, and toys, creating an immersive rolling environment. Scharf himself drove Suprema Ultima Deluxa cross-country to an exhibition at a Los Angeles Gallery. It became the first vehicle in his Karbombz series of customized art cars.

13
1986

Keith Haring

Untitled (Art Car), 1986
1963 Buick Special

KEITH HARING’s distinctive visual language—bold lines, dancing figures, and rhythmic patterns—first emerged in the New York City subways in the early 1980s, blurring the boundaries between fine art and street culture. Painted in 1986, his Buick exemplifies Haring’s willingness to consider any surface or object as a canvas for his art. As with much of his 3D work, the fluid lines interact with the curves of the car itself, creating a buoyant interplay between art and object. With its playful, graffiti-inspired style, Haring’s Buick attests to the vibrant intersection of art and urban culture in 1980s New York City.

14
1986

Robert Rauschenberg

BMW Art Car 6, 1986
BMW 635 CSi

ROBERT RAUSCHENBERG (b. 1925, Port Arthur, TX–d. 2008, Captiva, FL) was a leading figure in postwar American art. He was best known for his “Combines”—works that incorporate found objects with other art materials to blur the line between painting and sculpture. In 1986, Rauschenberg created the sixth BMW Art Car—the first to incorporate photographic imagery directly onto the car. One side of the car features an odalisque by the neoclassical French painter Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres (above). The other features 16th-century Italian artist Agnolo Bronzino’s painting Man of the World (left), with wheel covers depicting antique plates. Melding photographic imagery, traditional art history, and a high-performance machine, Rauschenberg’s BMW suggests that culture and technology are in constant motion.

15
1990s
1990

Jean Tinguely

Shuttlecock, 1990
Welded Sculpture: Iron, motor-cycle parts, electric motor

JEAN TINGUELY (b. 1925, Fribourg, Switzerland–d. 1991, Bern, Switzerland) was a Swiss sculptor best known for kinetic, self-destructing machines that mock the solemnity of the art world and modern industrial society. A member of the Nouveau Réalisme movement, he fused engineering with a playful sense of chaos. In 1988 he personally decorated a sidecar raced by multiple European champion René Progin. Tinguely later deconstructed the entire vehicle, including the helmets worn by Progin and his copilot, to create the welded, motorized sculpture Shuttlecock (1990). Completed the year before his death, Tinguely’s witty assemblage of rising, rotating, and whirling parts has been likened to a frozen explosion.

16
1991

A.R. Penck

BMW Art Car 11, 1991
1991 BMW Z1

The art of Ralf Winkler, better known as A. R. PENCK (b. 1939, Dresden–d. 2017, Zürich), is based on an expressive visual vocabulary that he dubbed “Standart.” It features simple pictographic symbols and abstract shapes that bring to mind prehistoric cave paintings, including the human figures he called “matchstick men.” Penck’s symbolic imagery covers the 11th BMW Art Car. On one side, a matchstick man with a spear hunts down an abstract X over a wavy line that suggests a river. On the other, an alligator stretches between the wheels as a lion strides above, “Art on art, art on technology; that grabbed my attention,” Penck said about the car. “Particularly the idea of art on a 3D element.”

17
1991

Dr. Esther Mahlangu

BMW Art Car 12, 1991
1991 BMW 525i

Dr. ESTHER MAHLANGU (b. 1935, Middleburg, South Africa) is an internationally renowned contemporary artist. She is strongly influenced by the decorative house and wall painting traditions of her people, the Ndebele, which she began practicing as a ten-year-old. In 1991, Dr. Mahlangu became the first woman, first African, and first person of color to create an art car for BMW. Covered in the colorful geometric abstraction she is known for, Dr. Mahlangu’s intricately patterned BMW Art Car celebrates Ndebele culture and her own innovative vision as an artist.

18
1993

Bertrand Lavier

Giulietta (1993), 1993
1993 Alfa Romeo Alfetta QTV

BERTRAND LAVIER (b. 1949, Châtillon-sur-Seine, France) is a conceptual artist, painter, and sculptor, known for covering everyday objects with what he calls “van Gogh brushwork.” In 1993, he placed a smashed Alfetta GTV on a gallery pedestal. Presenting the wreck without alteration, Lavier lets the accident reshape the car’s form. The result pairs the intentional curves of Italian automotive design and the unplanned sculpture created by the accident’s impact. Pristine on its pedestal, Giulietta (1993) exists as both automotive corpse and artistic rebirth.

19
1993

Gabriel Orozco

La DS, 1993
1950s Citroën DS

In much of his art, GABRIEL OROZCO (b. 1962, Vera Cruz, Mexico) reveals the poetry in everyday objects, often through precise interventions. With La DS (1993), Orozco created a dramatically compressed version of a Citroën DS, a 1950s automotive icon of postwar French ingenuity. Cutting a longitudinal center section from the car, he reassembled the two halves to retain the illusion of a functional vehicle. Orozco has called La DS a “three-dimensional photograph,” and like a photograph, the slimmed-down car flattens three-dimensional space—playing physical perception against the memory of how a car should look and function.

20
1995

César

Compression Voiture Venis, 1995
Compressed car, make and model unknown

CÉSAR (aka César Baldaccini, b. 1921, Marseille, France–d. 1998, Paris) was an innovator in the field of automotive art. Early in his career he made sculptures of welded scrap metal, but on a visit to a scrapyard he discovered the hydraulic crushing machine used to compress cars for disposal. He began using a hydraulic crusher to create the sculptures he called Compressions. The graceful lines of Compression Voiture Venise (1995), made a few years before his death, reflect César’s pioneering work in this unusual sculptural medium.

21
1995

David Hockney

BMW Art Car 14, 1995
1995 BMW 850 CSi

“I thought it would be a good idea to show the car as if one could see inside,” DAVID HOCKNEY (b. 1937, Bradford, England) said of his BMW Art Car, the 14th in the series. Accordingly, the driver’s side door sports silhouettes of a driver and the steering column, with one of Hockney’s beloved dachshunds attentive in the back. Painted shapes on the hood recall engine intake manifolds, and angled lines on white curves suggest the motion of air over the wheels. “Traveling around in a car means experiencing landscapes,” Hockney has said, and the car’s swaths of green are a nod to that thought. “The car has wonderful contours and I followed them,” he said. “It was lots of fun.”

22
1997

Sylvie Fleury

Skin Crime #3 (Givenchy 318), 1997
Crushed Fiat

The art of SYLVIE FLEURY (b. 1961, Geneva, Switzerland) deftly navigates the territories of luxury, consumerism, and gender politics. In Skin Crime 3 (Givenchy 318) (1997), part of her Skin Crime series, Fleury transforms a sports car—that enduring symbol of masculine power—into a compressed form that deliberately undermines its usual association with speed and status. Coated in the pink of a nail polish by international fashion and cosmetics powerhouse Givenchy, Skin Crime 3 is a slyly subversive contribution to the genre of automotive sculpture.

23
1999

Jenny Holzer

BMW Art Car 15, 1999
1999 BMW V12 LMR

JENNY HOLZER (b. 1950, Gallipolis, Ohio) is an American conceptual artist known for her use of text as art, and for introducing provocative, poetic, and political statements into public spaces. “Protect me from what I want” is one of the phrases adorning Holzer’s contribution to the BMW Art Car series, created in 1999. Holzer used chrome lettering and phosphorescent paint to cover the BMW V12 LMR racer with excerpts from her Truisms and Survival series. The chrome lettering reflected the sky during the car’s daytime races, and the phosphorescent paint glowed ghostly blue on nighttime runs—ensuring that BMW’s distinctive colors remained visible throughout the vehicle’s demanding 24-hour Le Mans race.

24
1999

Chen Zhen

Perseverance of Regeneration, 1999
Crashed car, toy cars, silicon, paint

CHEN ZHEN (b. 1955, Shanghai, China–d. 2000, Paris) was a Chinese-French conceptual artist who countered society’s increasing consumerism with works that explored healing, transformation, and transcendence. The tension between decay and vitality was central to Chen’s practice. In Perseverance of Regeneration (1999), a matte black car is swarmed by dozens of toy vehicles that cluster and bulge at the windows. Creating grotesque protrusions, the tiny objects suggest both infestation and rebirth. Created a year before Chen’s untimely death, Perseverance of Regeneration is a meditation on transformation and renewal.

25
2000s
2000

Damien Hirst

Untitled (Spot Mini), 2000
Mini Cooper

DAMIEN HIRST (b. 1965, Bristol, United Kingdom) is a British multidisciplinary artist known for provocative explorations of mortality, beauty, and belief systems. Untitled (Spot Mini) (2000) extends his Pharmaceutical series, begun in 1986, in which seemingly simple arrangements of colored spots probe complex questions about art, science, and mass production. Like his paintings in this series, the car is an exploration of color theory and mechanical reproduction: each spot is precisely uniform in size, no color is repeated, and the spaces between the dots are equal to their diameter.

26
2000–2011

Walter De Maria

Bel Air Trilogy, 2000-2011
Three 1955 Chevrolet Bel Air two-tone hardtops, stainless steel rods

Acclaimed for minimalist works and land art, WALTER DE MARIA (b. 1935, Albany, California–d. 2013, Los Angeles) brought precision and geometric rigor to his Bel Air Trilogy (2000-2011). Taking three identical 1955 Chevrolet Bel Air hardtops—iconic symbols of postwar American prosperity and design—De Maria transformed them through a violent, elegant intervention. Each vehicle is penetrated by a twelve-foot stainless steel rod that runs through the passenger compartment. The three rods differ in cross-section—square, circle, and triangle—in a geometric progression that is a recurring motif in De Maria’s work. Bel Air Trilogy reflects De Maria’s ability to create tension between precision and destruction, and between beauty and violence.

27
2001

Franz West

Untitled (La Limousine Bleu), 2002
MAK ART Edition (print run of 120 + 20 APs)

Known for humorous, playfully provocative sculptures, FRANZ WEST (b. 1947, Vienna, Austria–d. 2012, Vienna, Austria) never learned to drive but had a lifelong fascination with luxury cars. In his famous 2001 performance Par Bleu, West arranged for quarts of shocking pink paint to be poured over a Maserati Quattroporte during the opening of his exhibition at Vienna’s Museum of Applied Arts (MAK). The performance scandalized Vienna’s cultural elite and revealed West’s knack for questioning not only the nature of art but its relationship to luxury, value, and institutional validation.

28
2002

Futura

Untitled (Art Car), 2002
1976 BMW

FUTURA (formerly known as Futura 2000, b. 1955, New York City) is a multidisciplinary artist who emerged from the 1970s New York graffiti scene. About his Untitled (Art Car) (2002), he writes: “my love for the BMW 2002, the classic compact sports car I selected to paint, dates back to my first trip to EUROPE when I actually saw the vehicle in PARIS back in the early ’80s.” But, he adds, “the numerical significance is what has always attracted me. As the name FUTURA 2000 arrives via influences from the film 2001 A SPACE ODYSSEY, the BMW 2002 was the obvious next element in the numerical TRILOGY.” The car’s camouflage design is a nod to Futura’s time in the military, punctuated with his signature (opposite).

29
2002

Damián Ortega

Cosmic Thing, 2002
1983 Volkswagen Beetle, stainless steel wire, acrylic

Known for deconstructing everyday objects to explore themes of consumption, globalization, and cultural identity, DAMIÁN ORTEGA (b. 1967, Mexico City) began his career as a political cartoonist before becoming one of Mexico’s most prominent artists. In Cosmic Thing (2002), he meticulously disassembles a 1983 Volkswagen Beetle—manufactured in Mexico since the 1970s—and suspends its components in an exploded-diagram formation that reveals the car’s internal logic. A celebration of DIY car culture in Mexico City, where Beetles were prized for their simple mechanics and available parts, Cosmic Thing is also a critique of mass production, consumption, and the global flow of goods and technologies.

30
2003

Elmgreen & Dragset

Short Cut, 2003
1980s Fiat Uno, modified camping caravan, mixed media

Collaborating since 1995, MICHAEL ELMGREEN and INGAR DRAGSET are known for provocative works that challenge institutional and social structures through architectural interventions and sculptural displacements. Short Cut is a dramatic site-specific installation commissioned by Fondazione Nicola Trussardi for Milan’s historic Galleria Vittorio Emanuele. The work features a white Fiat Uno towing a camping caravan, which appears to have burst through the shopping arcade’s ornate marble floor, creating the illusion of an impossible journey from beneath the earth’s surface. Through meticulous attention to detail, including collaboration with Italian mosaic restorers to recreate and “damage” the historic floor patterns, the artists achieve a striking trompe l’oeil effect that sparked controversy and wonder.

31
2003

Subodh Gupta

Doot II, 2003–2009
Aluminum

Contemporary Indian artist SUBODH GUPTA (b. 1964, Khagaul, India) is known for creating sculptures and installations out of everyday objects of life in India, such as bicycles, milk pails, and kitchen utensils. In Doot II (2003–2009), Gupta casts the Hindustan Ambassador car—once the symbol of official India—in pure aluminum. Weighing more than the original car, Gupta’s work is monumental and completely opaque. A ghostly transformation of an iconic Indian vehicle, Doot II is a powerful meditation on India’s shifting identity between tradition and modernity.

32
2005

Erwin Wurm

Convertible Fat Car (Porsche), 2005
Porsche Carrera, mixed media

ERWIN WURM (b. 1954, Bruck an der Mur, Austria) has consistently expanded the concept of what can be considered sculpture. With his 2005 Convertible Fat Car (Porsche), he addresses the obesity epidemic in the United States by transforming a familiar symbol of sleek mobility and status into an organic, swollen form. Using polyurethane and styrofoam, he distorts the exterior shape of the car to resemble drooping layers of fat. “I was not satisfied with just making the good-looking works. I also wanted to make bad or ugly versions that lend themselves to a whole range of psychological states: embarrassment, ridicule or stupidity,” he has said. With Convertible Fat Car (Porsche), Wurm examines the uneasy relationship between power, wealth, and body image, critiquing a culture that simultaneously idealizes thinness and promotes overconsumption.

33
2008

Erwin Wurm

Renault 25-1991, 2008
1991 Renault 25, mixed media

In 2008, ERWIN WURM returned to the automobile as a sculptural object with Renault 25-1991. Designed at a slant, it resembles a cartoon car going around a turn at high speed. No stranger to incorporating humor in his work, Wurm uses absurdity as a tool to capture the viewer’s attention and encourage close examination. “I’m not a humorous person when I do art. I don’t step in front of a piece of clay and start to laugh,” he has said. “Another perspective on this reality makes people laugh.” The tension between seriousness and play underscores Wurm’s broader exploration of how everyday objects, especially the automobile, shape human experience. “I think no other object changes life as dramatically as a car. When we are driving it is protecting us. It is a form of representation. We can define ourselves with a car.”

34
2009

Zaha Hadid

Z.Car-II, 2008
Lightweight carbon, fiber composite, expanded polystyrene, polyurethane, car paint, rubber tires

ZAHA HADID (b. 1950 Baghdad, Iraq–d. 2016, Miami, Florida) was a visionary Iraqi-British architect, internationally acclaimed for her groundbreaking contributions to contemporary architecture. Hadid’s Z.Car-II (2008) is a compact, zero-emissions two-seater, powered by rechargeable lithium-ion batteries and electric in-wheel motors. Achieving remarkable spatial efficiency through a precise arrangement of mechanical and electrical components, the Z.Car-II embodies Hadid’s aesthetic of flowing lines and dynamic forms. The result is visually striking and environmentally conscious.

35
2009

Yinka Shonibare CBE RA

Crash Willy, 2009
Dutch wax resist cloth, mannequin, leather, fiberglass, metal

YINKA SHONIBARE CBE RA (b. 1962, London) explores questions of race, class, and identity in a range of media, including sculpture and installation. Crash Willy (2009) is a work in his Tableaux Vivants series, which interprets scenes from Western art history or literature—in this case, the suicide of Willy Loman in Arthur Miller’s classic play Death of a Salesman (1949). Constructed as part of the 2009 London gallery exhibition Willy Loman: The Rise and Fall, Crash Willy depicts the car’s driver in Shonibare’s characteristic style: a headless mannequin clad in Dutch wax resist cloth (also known as Ankara cloth), widely associated with parts of Africa.

36
2010s
2010

Jeff Koons

BMW Art Car 17, 2010
2010 BMW M3 GT2

JEFF KOONS (1955, York, Pennsylvania) is known for eye-catching artworks inspired by pop culture and everyday objects—most famously, the iconic Rabbit (1986), a stainless steel sculpture modeled on an inflatable Easter bunny. In designing his BMW Art Car, Koons aimed for maximum visual impact. No fewer than twenty different colors were used to create the vivid lines that flow over the car’s hood, body, and roof, gathering into an explosive burst of color and cartoonlike debris at the rear. Race cars like the M3 GT2 are “brimming with power and enormous energy,” Koons has said, and his design “is all about opening up to it completely.”

37
2010

John Chamberlain

Tastymozetta, 2010
Painted and chromed steel

JOHN CHAMBERLAIN (b. 1927, Rochester, Indiana–d. 2011, New York City) was one of the pioneers of automobile-based art. In the late 1950s Chamberlain began to incorporate scrap car parts into his sculptures, and in 1959 he shifted focus to works made entirely of crushed automobile parts welded together. Curator Susan Davidson, organizer of the Guggenheim Museum’s 2012 Chamberlain retrospective, has likened his crushed-car sculptures to collages, and—with their strong gestural lines and use of color—to three-dimensional works of Abstract Expressionism. Created in the year before his death, Tastymozzetta (2010) exemplifies his approach to automobile art.

38
2011

Kanye West & Jay-Z

Untitled, 2011
2004 Maybach 57, customized for the music video “Otis”

In 2011, rap music stars JAY-Z (b. 1969, Brooklyn) and KANYE WEST (b. 1977, Atlanta) released Watch the Throne, their first album together. One of the album’s tracks, “Otis,” opens with a sampling of Otis Redding’s “Try a Little Tenderness,” followed by the two stars trading off verses about wealth and fame. In the “Otis” music video, they rap as a 2004 Maybach 57—an ultra-luxury vehicle with an eyepopping price tag—is blowtorched, sawn apart, and “transformed into a Frankenstein-esque muscle car” that “would have been suitable for the terrain in Mad Max,” as one critic wrote. Behind the wheel, the laughing rap stars put the stripped-down, powerful car through its paces.

39
2012

Richard Prince

Vanishing Point (The Artist Cut), 2012–2013
1969 Dodge Challenger

RICHARD PRINCE (b. 1949, Panama Canal Zone) is a conceptual artist whose work questions the authorship and ownership of visual imagery, often by rephotographing, copying, and manipulating the work of others. His art car Vanishing Point (The Artist Cut) (2012–2013) reflects Prince’s command of American iconography—in this case, the muscle car, a symbol of automotive freedom and defiance. Channeling the raw, road-race energy of the 1971 cult film Vanishing Point, Prince interprets the Dodge Challenger—an iconic muscle car built for speed and spectacle—as a work of art, presenting it in an audaciously new context.

40
2014

Lars Fisk

Dodge Ball, 2014
Acrylic, vinyl, rubber, modified auto parts

“A suburban grocery getter” is how LARS FISK (b. 1970, Norwich, Vermont) describes the classic van that inspired Dodge Ball. The spherical sculpture is part of his ongoing Car Ball series, which includes everything from a UPS truck to a John Deere tractor. In creating these works, Fisk starts with found automotive parts, adding custom fabrications as needed and completing the exterior and interior surfaces himself. With a gold matte finish and woodgrain paneling that bring to mind iconic vans and station wagons of decades past, the orblike Dodge Ball is “a sort of perception shift,” Fisk says, “which is what I’m after in these works.”

41
2014 / 2017

Joseph Kosuth

Class Struggle, 2014/2017
1964 Rolls-Royce Silver Cloud III, mixed media

A pioneer of conceptual and installation art, JOSEPH KOSUTH (b. 1945, Toledo, Ohio) explores the relationship between words and objects and between language and meaning. About his art car Class Struggle (2014/2017), he writes: “When I went around the world by myself in the early’70s, I went to the Lenin Museum in Moscow. I went deluxe and had a private guide. When I came upon the Rolls-Royce, I turned to my Communist guide and said, with incredulity: ‘Lenin had a Rolls-Royce?’ And she very primly said, ‘Yes, but he drove it for the people.’ I loved it. So my Rolls, from 1965, called a Silver Cloud, is covered with quotes from Lenin, and inside are photos of his three Rolls (his staff had use of seven) framed in walnut to match the dashboard and mounted over the back window.” Though it was produced in 2017, by Kosuth’s preference Class Struggle is dated as 2014, the year he first conceived it.

42
2015

Ai Weiwei

Untitled (LEGO Car), 2015
BMW 5 Series

AI WEIWEI (b. 1957, Beijing, China) is a Chinese multidisciplinary artist and human rights activist, known for his outspoken critiques of authoritarianism. Ai’s Untitled (LEGO Car) (2015) began as a response to corporate censorship, when the LEGO company refused to sell him bricks for a planned artwork at the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne, Australia. Initially, a single car outside Ai’s Beijing studio collected LEGO donations from the public. That quickly expanded into an international network of BMWs serving as LEGO collection sites. Positioned outside cultural institutions worldwide, each car featured a modified sun roof with inch-wide (5 cm) openings, through which the public contributed LEGO bricks for Ai’s use.

43
2015

Lawrence Weiner

Untitled (Sow the Wind, Reap the Whirlwind), 2015
1949 Nash Metropolitan

LAWRENCE WEINER (b. 1942, New York City–d. 2021, New York City) was a pioneering figure in conceptual art, renowned for transforming language into visual statements. For his art car Sow the Wind, Reap the Whirlwind (2015), he chose to work with a 1949 Nash Metropolitan, a modestly sized economy car. Rendered in his characteristic bold, sans-serif typographic font, the phrase of the title wraps around the car with prophetic weight. In combining a profound biblical warning with an everyday car from America’s optimistic postwar era, Weiner created a mobile meditation on cause and effect, and on choices and consequences.

44
2016

John Baldessari

BMW Art Car 19, 2016
2016 BMW M6 GTLM

In creating the 19th BMW Art Car, conceptual artist JOHN BALDESSARI (b. 1931, National City, California–d. 2020, Venice, California) “entered uncharted territory,” he said, “not just in terms of the subject, but also moving from two- to three-dimensional art.” In the process, “the ideas all came at once: for instance, the red dot on the roof, so you can see it from above, FAST on one side” of the car and a two-dimensional picture of the car itself on the other. For Baldessari, the finished work “turned out playfully satirical, but it also highlights some of the trademark ideas that I use,” like the colorful dots. “So you can say, the BMW Art Car is definitely a typical Baldessari and the fastest artwork I ever created!”

45
2016

Peter Halley

Untitled (Art Car), 2016
Sculpted three-dimensional object, laminate on wood

PETER HALLEY (b. 1953, New York City, New York) is an American painter and writer known for vibrant geometric abstractions that critique modern social structures. Emerging in the 1980s, Halley’s work features Day-Glo colors and rigid forms that he calls “cells” and “conduits,” symbolizing isolation and control within urban and digital life. “After mulling it over, I decided I didn’t really want to identify with any particular car brand,” Halley has said about his Untitled (Art Car) (2016). Instead, he opted to “take elements from the vocabulary of my paintings and create an absurd, boxy car—almost like a cartoon car.”

46
2016

Shirin Neshat

Untitled (Art Car), 2016
1966 Mercedes Benz 280SE, video, projected installation

SHIRIN NESHAT (b. 1957, Qazvin, Iran) is an Iranian- American visual artist and filmmaker acclaimed for her powerful explorations of identity, gender, and cultural dynamics within Islamic societies. Her Untitled (Art Car), she says, “aims to create a cinematic experience by projecting a short film”—Neshat’s Roja (2016)—“onto a vehicle’s windows, allowing the narrative to unfold as viewers walk around the car. Each window reveals specific moments and scenes, engaging the audience from multiple perspectives.” Neshat’s choice of car, a Mercedes-Benz 280SE, “was an esthetic decision, as the narrative is set in the past, and the vehicle’s design evokes a nostalgic, timeless quality that complements the story’s historical tone.”

47
2016

Jonas Wood

Untitled (Art Car), 2016
Customized 1993 Volvo 240

JONAS WOOD (b. 1977, Boston, Massachusetts) creates cinematic, stage-like paintings, drawings, and prints that are dense with texture, vividly imagined, and yet oddly familiar. In his Untitled (Art Car) (2016), Wood applies his signature style to a 1993 Volvo 240, covering the exterior in a variegated pattern that brings to mind outsized wood grain or safari-style tiger stripes. The result is an eye-catching clash of worlds: the Volvo 240’s reputation for safety and sensibility meeting the unexpectedly adventurous energy of Wood’s vision.

48
2016

Rashid Johnson

Untitled (Soul on Ice), 2016
1987 Saab, mixed media

RASHID JOHNSON (b. 1977, Chicago, Illinois) is an American multidisciplinary artist whose work spans photography, sculpture, painting, film, and installation. He explores themes of race, identity, and personal history, often incorporating materials like shea butter, black soap, and ceramic tile to evoke narratives rooted in African American culture. For the art car Untitled (Soul on Ice) (2016), Johnson chose a Saab similar to one that his mother had driven in Chicago. Incorporating white ceramic tile, black soap, and wax, Untitled (Soul on Ice) is filled with copies of Soul on Ice, the influential book of essays published in 1968 by activist and Black Panther Party leader Eldridge Cleaver.

49
2017

Marilyn Minter

Green Pink Caviar Pacer, 2017
1976 AMC Pacer, chrome vinyl wrap, rear-projection painted windows with digital video projections

In painting, photography, and video, MARILYN MINTER (b. 1948, Shreveport, Louisiana) creates hyperreal explorations of beauty, desire, and the everyday realities of the body. In her voyeuristic, near-hallucinogenic video Green Pink Caviar (2009), a woman’s mouth is shown in extreme close-up, pressed against glass as she licks, sucks, and spits out various substances, simultaneously alluring and repulsive. In Green Mint Caviar Pacer (2017), Minter projects the video from inside a 1976 AMC Pacer. Once heralded for its futuristic design, the Pacer is itself a comment on the nature of desire and obsolescence, and its transformation epitomizes Minter’s provocative take on glamour and consumption.

50
2017

Carmen Herrera

Black/White Car, 2017
1964 Lincoln Continental

CARMEN HERRERA (b. 1915, Havana, Cuba – d. 2022, New York City) was a Cuban-American painter whose distinctive style—with its sharp lines, vibrant colors, and precise forms—embodies a rigorous geometric abstraction and minimalism. Despite creating art for decades, Herrera sold her first painting at the age of 89 and received her first major museum retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 2016, at the age of 101. Created on a Lincoln Continental, her Black/White Car (2017) is a bold, starkly reductive variation on a color combination that appears frequently in her work.

51
2017

Keith Sonnier

Untitled (Flocked), 2017
1950 Oldsmobile 88, neon with mixed media

KEITH SONNIER (b. 1941, Mamou, Louisiana–d. 2020, Southampton, New York) was an American artist whose pioneering use of unconventional materials expanded the concept of sculpture in the late 1960s. Neon enabled him to draw lines in space and in color, and it quickly became a signature medium. Other key materials included latex paint embedded with flocking—particles of fiber that give surfaces a velvety, tactile appearance. Those elements come together in Sonnier’s Untitled (Flocked) (2017), a 1950s Oldsmobile 88 coupe with whitewall tires and an exterior covered in soft gray flocking, gently illuminated from within by green neon.

52
2017

Barbara Kruger

Untitled (School), 2017
School Bus, vinyl wrap

With a background in graphic design, BARBARA KRUGER (b. 1945, Newark, New Jersey) creates bold, text-driven works that tackle issues of feminism, consumerism, and power dynamics in contemporary society. Kruger created Untitled (School) (2017) for the Performa Biennial in New York City. Her interventions transformed the classic yellow school bus into a mobile site of cultural critique, carrying thought-provoking phrases like “Know Nothing. Believe Anything. Forget Everything” and “Up Is Down, Right Is Wrong, Nasty Is Nice.” The bus is part of a series of mobile works by Kruger dating back to the 1990s, when she first wrapped a New York City bus in her text-based art.

53
2017

JR & Agnès Varda

Camion Inside Out (Inside Out Truck), 2015
Customized 2005 Ford E-350 Super Duty Extended Passenger Van

In 2017, iconic New Wave filmmaker AGNÈS VARDA, then 89, joined acclaimed French photographer-artist JR on a road trip through France. Made to resemble a giant camera, the truck they traveled in had been created for JR’s long-running project, Inside Out. It was equipped with a photo booth and a large-scale photographic printer, which the duo used to make mural-sized images of the people they met on their journey, “magnifying and honoring them on a scale usually reserved for public and historic figures,” as the New Yorker wrote. The trip was documented in the Oscar-nominated movie Visages Villages (Faces Places), which the New York Times called “a powerful, complex and radical work.”

54
2018

Daniel Arsham

Eroded Ferarri, 2018
Steel, fiberglass, selenite, quartz

DANIEL ARSHAM (b. 1980, Cleveland, Ohio) is a multidisciplinary artist whose work spans sculpture, architecture, performance, and film. Eroded Ferrari (2018) is part of Arsham’s broader practice of “fictional archaeology,” in which he creates eroded versions of cultural artifacts, challenging our sense of permanence. Cast in quartz and selenite, the vehicle takes on the appearance of a fossilized artifact, its iconic form recognizable but destabilized by strategic erosion. In Arsham’s hands, a symbol of speed and luxury becomes a meditation on time and decay.

55
2018

Felipe Pantone

ULTRADYNAMIC, 2018
1994 Corvette, holographic film, spray paint

With roots in street art, FELIPE PANTONE (b. 1986, Buenos Aires, Argentina) has crafted a signature visual language that emphasizes bold colors, optical patterns, and pixelated graphics. In creating his edition of three hand-painted art cars, Pantone chose to work with a 1994 Corvette, an iconic sportscar known for its sleek design. Rather than treating the car as simply a surface, Pantone’s design works in intimate dialogue with its curves and contours. Staggered stripes and pixelated rectangles surge across the bodywork, turning each vehicle into a study of motion itself. These are cars that appear to accelerate even while standing still.

56
2019

Ugo Rondinone

cloud car, 2019
Fiberglass, wood, metal, paint

UGO RONDINONE (b.1964, Locarno, Switzerland) is celebrated for an expansive body of work that blurs the boundaries between sculpture, painting, and installation art. His immersive installations invite viewers to contemplate what he calls “the ephemeral beauty of existence,” and to reflect on time, memory, transience, and emotion. For cloud car (2019), Rondinone created his own automotive form, a low-slung sportscar shape. Positioned on a small, barely discernible base, cloud car seems to hover in space—much like the clouds and sky that cover its surface.

57
2019

Hank Willis Thomas

A Suspension of Hostilities, 2019
1969 Dodge Charger

HANK WILLIS THOMAS (b. 1976, Plainfield, New Jersey) is an American conceptual artist whose work explores race, identity, history, and the visual language of advertising. As an African American boy growing up in New York, The Dukes of Hazzard was his favorite television show, and a miniature of the show’s iconic “General Lee” Dodge Charger was a prized toy. Even in his household, he said, there was never a sense “that there was a problem with the context or the Confederate flag.” His sculpture, A Suspension of Hostilities, challenges the unquestioned acceptance of Confederate symbolism in American life by planting a replica of the “General Lee” headfirst in the ground, bringing its wild ride to a sudden end.

58
2020s
2020

Virgil Abloh

Mercedes-Benz x Virgil Abloh Project Geländewagen 1:3 Scale Maquette, 2020
Mercedes Benz G-Class SUV

Designer VIRGIL ABLOH (b. 1980, Rockford, Illinois–d. 2021, Chicago) established his own international fashion brand, Off-White, in 2013 before becoming artistic director of the Louis Vuitton menswear collection in 2018. In 2020, Abloh collaborated with Mercedes Benz on Project Geländewagen, a re-envisioning of its luxury G-Class SUV. Abloh imagined it as a racing car, stripping the interior down to its fundamentals and adding pops of color with cherry-red safety features and a bright blue roll bar and exhaust pipes. Abloh created the Mercedes Benz x Virgil Abloh Project Geländewagen 1:3 Scale Maquette (2020) as a unique artwork modeled on the full-size concept car. The vision, he said, was a car that’s “luxurious in a deconstructed way” and “runs away from the idea of perfection . . . to embrace the human touch.”

59
2024

Julie Mehretu

BMW Art Car 20, 2024
2024 BMW M Hybrid V8

When JULIE MEHRETU (b. 1970, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia) received a model of the BMW M Hybrid V-8 racer—the vehicle she would turn into the 20th BMW Art Car—she was working on the painting Everywhere (2021–23), a massive ten-foot by ten-foot canvas now at the Museum of Modern Art, New York. “I thought: What would happen if this car seemed to go through that painting and becomes affected by it,” she said. “The idea was to make a remix, a mash-up of the painting. I kept seeing that painting kind of dripping into the car.” Complex and multilayered, Mehretu’s Art Car captures what she calls the “blur and uncertainty” of our social moment—especially at racetrack speeds.

60
2024

Michelangelo Pistoletto

Untitled (Art Car), 2024
1955 Oldsmobile 88 Coupe

A founder of the Arte Povera movement, MICHELANGELO PISTOLETTO (b 1933, Biella, Italy) uses everyday materials to explore themes of perception and social transformation. Since 2003, Pistoletto has worked with the concept of Il Terzo Paradiso (the Third Paradise), a utopian coming together of the natural world and the world of human artifice. He symbolizes it with a reconfigured infinity sign, expanded to include a third, central circle, and with the mathematical statement “1 + 1 = 3.” Those symbols adorn the upper surfaces of Untitled (Art Car) (2023), with the sociopolitical opposites of “USA” and “Cuba”—where Pistoletto has presented several Third Paradise projects—written on the hood and trunk.

61
2024

Joshua Vides

93 ’TIL, 2024
1993 Porsche Carrera 911 / Base 2

JOSHUA VIDES (b. 1989, Rialto, California) is best known for a bold, black-and-white graphic style that transforms real objects into what appear to be hand-drawn illustrations. Coining the concept “Reality to Idea,” Vides aims to take “everything back to its origin, which is pen and paper.” With 93 ’TIL, thick, black contour lines outline each panel, seam, and curve of this 1993 Porsche Carrera, flattening the three-dimensional vehicle into an optical illusion that resembles a comic strip or sketchbook page. Shaped by graffiti and streetwear culture, Vides’s unique style reflects his upbringing on the outskirts of Los Angeles, and he hopes to reach wide audiences, especially young people. “I wanted to create items that were accessible to kids coming to the museum for the first time,” he says, “items that could inspire them and create excitement.’”

62
2024

Olafur Eliasson

Your compilation-of-self-car, 2024
Lotus Exige

OLAFUR ELIASSON (b. 1967, Copenhagen, Denmark) is a Danish–Icelandic artist known for immersive installations that merge art, science, and environmental awareness. His work often employs elemental materials such as light, water, and air temperature—notably The Weather Project, a 2003 installation that brought a record-breaking 2 million visitors to the Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. Eliasson applies a similar sensibility to Your compilation-of-self car (2024). He covers a high-performance sports car, the Lotus Exige, in a pattern that recalls spatial heat maps—a type of graphic seen with increasing frequency in relation to climate change and natural disasters.

63
2024

Shepard Fairey

Untitled (Art Car), 2024
1937 Packard 4-door Sedan

SHEPARD FAIREY (b. 1970, Charleston, South Carolina) is perhaps best known for designing the iconic “Hope” poster for Barack Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign. Fairey uses high-recognition imagery, striking forms, and color to merge street art with political messaging. Created on a 1937 Packard Touring Sedan, his Art Car contrasts two musical perspectives on capitalism. One side, celebrating wealth and opulence, features hip-hop lyrics from artists such as Slick Rick, Chuck D of Public Enemy, and The Notorious B.I.G. The other, critiquing consumerism and power, draws on punk-music lyrics from Joe Strummer of The Clash, Jello Biafra of Dead Kennedys, and Jamie Reid’s work with the Sex Pistols. Rendered in intricate metallic gold patterns, the car pairs the visual language of luxury with pointed social commentary, turning a symbol of excess into a layered reflection on power and consumption.

64
2025

Nina Chanel Abney

In Case of Emergency, 2025
1970 Chevrolet C10

NINA CHANEL ABNEY (b. 1982, Chicago, Illinois) is a contemporary American artist known for vibrant graphic compositions that confront themes of race, gender, politics, and pop culture. About In Case of Emergency (2025), Abney writes: “The pickup truck has long been embedded in America’s visual and cultural landscape, a symbol of rural labor, mobility, and, for many Black Americans, a site of terror. Pickup trucks began to symbolize racialized terror as early as the 1920s and 1930s, when they were used in acts of mob violence, lynching transport, and intimidation across the Jim Crow South. From that era through the present day, the pickup has often been weaponized as an emblem of white supremacy, used in acts of intimidation, violence, and surveillance against Black and brown bodies. Its image, headlights approaching down a dark road, flags flying from the bed, continues to carry that legacy in subtle and overt ways. In transforming this vehicle, I wanted to reclaim something historically tied to fear and turn it into a vessel of liberation and protection. Painted in the colors of the Pan-African flag, red for the blood, black for the people, and green for the land, the truck becomes a “rescue vehicle” for the present moment. The bold graphics, faces, and hand motifs signal both alarm and care, a call to action and a gesture of defense. In these times, when Black and brown communities continue to face systemic violence and political erasure, In Case of Emergency reimagines the pickup not as a threat, but as a promise, an emergency response unit for collective survival, solidarity, and self-determination.”

65

End of wall

“The world is changing rapidly, and as essential as the automobile is today, it’s impossible to know what form transportation will take in a hundred or two hundred years—or how, in that distant future, the works in this book will be regarded.”

—Larry Warsh, New York City, 2026
